subtype: Approach: listing skills and free hours first [Thinking]
passage:
Monday. Vasudha tore a page from the notebook and wrote two columns. Left: things I can do. Tutoring maths, poster design, typing in two scripts. Right: hours. Classes fill mornings, labs take Tuesday and Thursday, and after subtracting sleep, meals and travel, about eight hours a week remain. "Anything bigger than that is fantasy," Vasudha told Seema.

Wednesday. Ideas came and each was tested against the eight hours. A full-time delivery job? No. Weekend poster jobs? Yes, roughly three hours each.

Sunday. On the wall above the desk now hung a small card: poster work, two evenings, tutoring one hour on Saturday. Seema said it looked like something Vasudha could actually keep going.

qa.q: About how many free hours a week did Vasudha find?
qa.a: About eight hours a week remained after classes, labs, sleep, meals and travel.

qa.q: What did Vasudha think of ideas bigger than the free hours?
qa.a: Vasudha felt firm and a little anxious, thinking anything bigger than the eight hours was fantasy, and tested each idea against the real time.

qa.q: What could Vasudha try if the tutoring takes longer than planned, and why?
qa.a: Vasudha could shrink the poster work for that week, because the plan stays inside the same eight hours.

qa.q: How might Seema see Vasudha's card on the wall?
qa.a: Seema saw something practical that Vasudha could keep up, since it matched the time available.

grounding: A student lists skills and counts free hours after classes so a side-income idea fits real time.

subtype: Approach: testing with one paying client [Action]
passage: In the small town of Pilibhit, Preeti had a laptop, a free design app and no customers. She walked to the stationery shop on the corner, where Jasleen ran the counter, and offered to design a poster for the new notebook offer, at a modest price. Jasleen agreed to try. It took Preeti nearly five hours, far longer than guessed, mostly because Jasleen wanted three colours changed. Preeti wrote the hours down. Jasleen also asked whether it could be printed on a bigger sheet, a question Preeti had never thought of. Before telling anyone else, Preeti made a short list: hours taken, what the client asked, and what price would be fair next time.

qa.q: How long did the first poster take Preeti?
qa.a: The first poster took Preeti nearly five hours.

qa.q: What did Preeti realise from the first job?
qa.a: Preeti felt surprised, since the job took far longer than guessed and a customer asked things such as bigger print sizes that Preeti had not thought of.

qa.q: What could Preeti do next before advertising widely, and why?
qa.a: Preeti could try a second small job at a fairer rate, because one more test shows if the time and price are steady.

qa.q: How might Jasleen see the offer from a student with no other clients?
qa.a: Jasleen may feel it is a low-risk chance to try something new and to get a poster made at a modest price.

grounding: A student offers to design posters for one local shop, sees how long it really takes and learns what customers ask before promoting widely.

passage: Friday night. Three videos this week showed young people with fancy phones saying they earn from trading and paid schemes with no skill needed. Today I joined a group, paid the entry fee from my savings, and told nobody, not even Gargi, because she would ask questions. The people in the group post screenshots of gains, and I am not sure which are real. I still don't understand how anyone earns, only that I have to bring in two friends to unlock the next level. I lost a full afternoon watching the group chat instead of studying. I don't feel excited anymore. I feel foolish. Tomorrow I will stop paying anything more and speak to my parents. Nandini

qa.q: What did Nandini pay for from savings?
qa.a: Nandini paid the entry fee for the group from savings.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel by the end of the entry?
qa.a: Nandini no longer felt excited and felt foolish, and had lost an afternoon watching the group chat.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Nandini have used before joining, and why?
qa.a: Nandini could have asked how the money was actually earned and talked to Gargi or a parent first, because real earnings can be explained plainly.

qa.q: How might Gargi feel if she learned Nandini had told her nothing?
qa.a: Gargi may feel worried and a bit hurt, since she would have asked the questions that could have stopped the joining.

grounding: A student joins a scheme from videos claiming easy earnings without checking, risking savings and time and learning no real skill.

subtype: Approach: budget and pricing with cost tracking [Thinking]
passage:
Kashish: So how much will you charge for a poster?

Pankaj: I'm working it out. Let me write it down.

Kashish: Just say a number.

Pankaj: If I guess I'll lose money. Data for the design app, the bus to the print shop, two hours per poster. If I want a fair hour of my time, that's another chunk.

Kashish: And?

Pankaj: My first price of two hundred barely pays for data and travel. I'd be working for free.

Kashish: Wow. I would have said two hundred and been happy.

Pankaj: So did I, an hour ago. Now it's three fifty, and I can explain why.

Kashish: Do people pay that?

Pankaj: We'll see. At least I know my floor.

qa.q: What did the first price of two hundred barely cover?
qa.a: The first price of two hundred barely covered data and travel.

qa.q: What did Pankaj realise while working out the costs?
qa.a: Pankaj felt startled to realise that the first price left no pay for time, so the work would be free, and the price needed to change.

qa.q: What could Pankaj do if customers say three fifty is too high, and why?
qa.a: Pankaj could offer a simpler poster at a lower price, since the floor is known and the job can be trimmed.

qa.q: How might Kashish see the change from a guessed number to a worked one?
qa.a: Kashish may feel surprised and a bit impressed, since Kashish would have accepted two hundred without thinking.

grounding: A student works out costs, time per job and a fair hourly rate, and notices the first price barely covers data and travel.

passage: My name is Pankaj, and last term I said yes to five tutoring batches because the money looked good. By the second week I was teaching until nine at night, then trying to do my own assignments. I missed two morning lectures. I fell asleep during a lab. My friend Shankar lent me his notes and asked, kindly, if I was okay. I said the money was worth it. Then the internal test results came out and my marks had dropped in three subjects. The extra income for the month had been real. But so was the cost, and I only saw it when the sheet arrived. I had been counting money and forgetting everything else.

qa.q: How many tutoring batches did Pankaj take?
qa.a: Pankaj took five tutoring batches.

qa.q: What did Pankaj feel when the test results came out?
qa.a: Pankaj felt dismayed at the drop in marks, and realised the cost had been forgotten while counting money.

qa.q: What could Pankaj do next term, and why?
qa.a: Pankaj could limit the batches to what the timetable allows and keep evenings before tests free, because the marks are the reason for studying.

qa.q: How might Shankar see Pankaj's answer that the money was worth it?
qa.a: Shankar was probably worried and unsure how to help, since a friend who is tired and missing lectures says everything is fine.

grounding: A student takes five tutoring batches, attendance and sleep suffer and marks fall, so the extra income has a real cost.

passage: Thomas leaned on the counter of the bookshop and said to Joseph, "I taught after college too, and I nearly ruined my degree. Then I made a rule. Ten hours a week, no more. Tuesday and Thursday evenings, six to eight, and Saturday morning. I wrote it on the wall calendar in red. Exam weeks stayed clear, all of them. If a parent asked for an extra class, I said, 'Sorry, that slot is not mine.' It felt hard the first month. After that it was easy." Thomas straightened a pile of books. "The money kept coming, and my studies were never eaten up. A boundary is just a decision you make once, so you don't have to make it every day."

qa.q: How many hours a week did Thomas allow for paid work?
qa.a: Thomas allowed ten hours a week.

qa.q: What did Thomas feel in the first month of the rule?
qa.a: Thomas felt uncomfortable holding the rule in the first month, as it felt hard, but after that it became easy.

qa.q: What could Joseph do to set a personal limit, and why?
qa.a: Joseph could write a personal weekly limit on a wall calendar and mark exam weeks clear, since a written rule is easier to keep.

qa.q: How might a parent who wanted an extra class have seen Thomas's answer?
qa.a: The parent may have felt disappointed but also learned that the slots were fixed, which makes future requests clearer.

grounding: An elder recalls limiting paid work to ten hours a week in fixed evening slots and keeping exam weeks free.

subtype: Approach: reframing income as skill building [Thinking]
passage:
Thursday. Sabina was offered two jobs: data entry at a good hourly rate, or building a website for a small tailor's shop for slightly less. She thought aloud to Urmila over tea. "Data entry pays now and gives me nothing after. The website pays a bit less, but I'd have something to show. A page online, a real client, a line in my portfolio."

Saturday. She chose the website. The shop wanted the opening hours, a gallery and a phone button.

Two months later. Sabina applied for a summer internship and put the tailor's website link at the top of the application. The interviewer asked about it first. Urmila said, "Told you it was worth the difference."

qa.q: What did the tailor's shop want on the website?
qa.a: The shop wanted the opening hours, a gallery and a phone button on the website.

qa.q: What was Sabina thinking when comparing the two jobs?
qa.a: Sabina felt torn but hopeful, reasoning that data entry pays now but leaves nothing afterwards, while the website pays slightly less and adds to a portfolio.

qa.q: What could Sabina try if the website work stops, and why?
qa.a: Sabina could offer the shop a small monthly update, because it keeps an ongoing client and new work for the portfolio.

qa.q: How might Urmila see Sabina's choice of the lower-paying job?
qa.a: Urmila probably felt it was a sound choice, and said it was worth the difference after the interviewer asked about the site. 🙂

grounding: A student picks paid work that also builds a portfolio, such as small website jobs, rather than chasing only the highest pay.

subtype: Approach: checking rules and honest dealing [Action]
passage: Sunaina read the college handbook twice before saying yes to her first paid job. The rule on page fourteen was clear: students may do paid work outside class hours, provided they declare it to the department. She filled the form the same evening. Samir, whose dad ran a print shop, had asked for a flyer design. Sunaina wrote the price and the delivery date on a small note, kept a folder with every draft, and sent the final file a day early. When Samir found a spelling mistake, she fixed it without charge and said sorry. A week later, two of Samir's neighbours messaged asking for the same designer. Sunaina had not advertised anywhere.

qa.q: On which page of the handbook did Sunaina find the rule?
qa.a: The rule was on page fourteen of the handbook.

qa.q: What did Sunaina feel on being asked by Samir's neighbours?
qa.a: Sunaina was probably pleased and encouraged, since the requests came without any advertising.

qa.q: What could Sunaina do to keep this going, and why?
qa.a: Sunaina could keep the note and folder system for every job, because clear records make later disputes and repeat work easier.

qa.q: How might Samir see the free fix and the early delivery?
qa.a: Samir probably trusts Sunaina and feels well served, which is why the neighbours were told about the designer.

grounding: A student checks campus rules allow paid work, keeps clear records and delivers what was promised, so trust spreads by word of mouth.

subtype: Approach: measuring results and dropping weak options [Revision]
passage: I'm Ayesha, and for a month I tried three kinds of side work: tutoring, small freelance edits, and data entry. It felt like a lot, so I wrote everything in a table with hours and money and worked out what I earned per hour. Tutoring came first, freelance edits were close, and data entry was far behind. I had been doing data entry because it was easy to find, not because it paid. Vasudha looked at the table over my shoulder and said, "So drop the worst one." I felt a small reluctance. I had already told the agency I would continue. But numbers are numbers. I sent a polite message the next morning and kept the other two.

qa.q: What three kinds of side work did Ayesha try?
qa.a: Ayesha tried tutoring, small freelance edits and data entry.

qa.q: How did Ayesha feel about dropping data entry?
qa.a: Ayesha felt a small reluctance because the agency had been told the work would continue, but the numbers were clear.

qa.q: What could Ayesha do with the time freed from data entry, and why?
qa.a: Ayesha could put it into tutoring or edits, since the table showed those pay better for each hour.

qa.q: How might Vasudha see Ayesha's table?
qa.a: Vasudha probably finds it simple and convincing, since the table made it easy to say to drop the worst one.

grounding: After a month a student compares hourly earnings across three side jobs and drops the one that pays least for the effort.

subtype: Approach: saving a fixed share as a buffer [Action]
passage: Tuition centre supervisor's note. Imran has taught two evening batches since August, and I noticed something unusual on payment days. Most of the young tutors go straight to the canteen. Imran opens a small notebook, takes out a third of the envelope and puts it into a tin marked "exams and emergencies". The rest is spent without guilt on food, bus fare and a film. Simran, a fellow tutor, asked about it and Imran said, "Then I never have to decide what to do with the whole amount." In October a sudden lab fee came up and Imran paid it from the tin without borrowing. I did not comment, but I have started suggesting the tin idea to the newer staff.

qa.q: What is written on the tin where Imran puts a third of each payment?
qa.a: The tin is marked exams and emergencies.

qa.q: What did Imran feel about spending the rest?
qa.a: Imran spent the rest without guilt, sure that the saved third was already set aside.

qa.q: What could Imran do if the tin fills up, and why?
qa.a: Imran could decide on a second small target such as books, because the habit stays the same while the goal changes.

qa.q: How might the supervisor see Imran's habit compared with other tutors?
qa.a: The supervisor seems impressed and a little surprised, and has started suggesting the idea to newer staff.

grounding: A student saves a fixed share of every payment for exam fees and emergencies and spends the rest, making income a steady support.
